newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan trade demands could backfire at APEC.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan trade demands could backfire at APEC.

text.p: Japan's insistence on protecting its investments abroad even while it drags its feet on freeing up farm imports at home could cost it a leadership role at this month's Asia-Pacific economic meetings in the Philippines.

Japan won plaudits as host of last year's Osaka summit of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum for adroitly steering the gathering through an emerging battle between developing and industrialised members of the 18-nation bloc.
It came up with a formula to keep APEC on track toward its goal of achieving trade and investment liberalisation by 2010 for industrialised members and 2020 for developing ones.
The Osaka formula allowed each member to draft its own Individual Action Plan for freeing trade and investment, rather than trying to reach a uniform, binding agreement encompassing all members.

The individual plans are to be unveiled in Manila at the APEC ministerial meeting on November 22-23. They will then be incorporated into a Collective Action Plan to be endorsed by the APEC leaders meeting at Subic Bay on November 25.
But Japan's own individual plan may fall widely short of expectations, especially in farm imports, Japanese commentators said.

While details of Japan's plan have not been revealed, it is unlikely to include any commitment to free up farm trade beyond promises made at the Uruguay Round of multilateral trade negotiations, government sources said.

"Japan's tariffs on farm and livestock products are still too high," said commentator Hiroaki Tsuji of the daily Asahi Shimbun. "On top of this, Japan still maintains quotas on rice and some fish products.

"One of the biggest impetuses to furthering APEC's momentum will be for Japan... to act as a locomotive in trade liberalisation and market-opening measures," Tsuji said. "Japan should be ready to hurt itself if it wants to contribute to a future Asia-Pacific union like the European Union."
Japan's main goal in this week's APEC meetings is to lay the groundwork for a uniform set of rules to protect foreign investment in the region, where Japan is one of the biggest investors.
"We must at least get this mentioned in the Subic Bay (summit) declaration," one government source said.

But by their nature, investment rules are anathema to many developing countries and if Japan pushes too hard, its reluctance to give ground on farm imports could be singled out as an example of a Japanese double standard.
APEC matters aside, Japan's biggest concern in Manila is how to mend frayed ties with China.

A row over disputed islands in the East China Sea -- called the Senkaku Islands by Japan and the Diaoyu Islands by China and Taiwan -- flared up this year after a Japanese nationalist group erected a make-shift lighthouse on one of the islands to underscore Japan's territorial claim.

China was also incensed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's visit to a war shrine in July. The Yasukuni Shrine is dedicated to Japan's 2.6 million war dead, including convicted war criminals such as former Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, Japan's World War Two leader.

Hashimoto has his first talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin in a bilateral meeting on Sunday afternoon after earlier talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton, Philippines President Fidel Ramos and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
In his talks with Jiang, Hashimoto may try to improve ties by releasing grants worth $60 million, frozen since August 1995 when China conducted an underground nuclear test.

APEC's members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
